text: Ada burned the birthday cake she had promised to bake for her neighbor's daughter, then, rushing, bought one from the shop and passed it off as her own. The girl had hugged her and said it was the best cake ever. Now, alone in her kitchen scrubbing the black pan, Ada kept seeing that small face. Her stomach turned each time. She had lied to a seven-year-old over a cake. She scrubbed harder than the pan needed. She thought about knocking on the neighbor's door and telling the truth, then pictured the girl's face again, and put the sponge down, and could not decide what she owed.

Milo had cooked dinner for his mother on her last visit and snapped at her when she offered to help. She had gone quiet and sat at the table with her hands folded. That was in March. Now she was in hospital and could not speak, and he stood in his kitchen chopping onions for no one, replaying that moment again and again. Why had he spoken to her like that. It would have cost him nothing to let her stir the pot. His hands slowed on the knife. He would give anything to take back those words and could not, and the weight of them sat on his chest.

On the crowded tram Oren had pretended not to see the old woman standing with her shopping bags, and kept his seat. At the next stop she had stumbled when the tram braked and fallen against the door. Other people helped her up. He had stared at his phone. Now, at his desk an hour later, he could not stop seeing her hand reaching for the rail. His face felt hot. It had been such a small thing to stand up. He kept going over it, the moment he chose not to, and each time his stomach twisted tighter, as if his body were trying to undo it.

Pia had been driving to work too fast, late again, when she clipped the wing mirror of a parked van and kept going. Nobody saw. All day the sound of that crack came back to her, the little spray of glass in her rearview. Someone would come out to that van and find it broken and have to pay to fix it. Her neck and shoulders were tight as wire. At lunch she could not eat. After work she drove back to the street, her heart thudding, and wrote a note with her number, and her hand shook as she slid it under the wiper.

Kai's sister called to say their father had asked for him again. Kai said he was busy with work, which was not true. He had not visited in six months, not since the argument, and every excuse he made grew thinner. After the call he sat staring at the phone. His father was eighty-three. He thought of him in the chair by the window, asking, and of himself here, doing nothing. His throat tightened and his chest felt heavy with it. He opened the train timetable and closed it, and opened it again, and knew he should have gone long ago.

Ines had missed her grandmother's ninetieth birthday call because she was at a party, and had meant to ring back the next day. She forgot. Three days later her mother called to say how long the old woman had waited by the phone that evening. Ines listened with her hand over her mouth. The picture of her grandmother sitting there, dressed up, the phone in her lap, would not leave her. Her face burned and her stomach sank. She rang at once, and her grandmother said never mind, never mind, and somehow that made it worse, far worse.

Esme had let her colleague take the fall for the lost client files. It had been her mistake, and she had stayed silent in the meeting while the manager read out his name. He had been moved to another team. Now she passed his old desk every morning, empty, a plant wilting on it. Each time her stomach lurched. At night she wrote emails to the manager explaining everything and deleted them before sending. The truth sat inside her like something swallowed wrong. She knew that every day she stayed quiet, she was choosing it all over again.

Bram had signed off on the safety check without looking, because it was Friday and he wanted to go home. On Monday a worker slipped on the loose platform and broke his wrist. Nobody connected it to him. Bram visited the man in hospital with a bag of oranges and could not look him in the eye. The man joked about his cast and thanked him for coming. Bram smiled and nodded, and on the drive home he had to pull over, his hands trembling on the wheel, because he knew exactly whose signature was on that sheet.

Lale had sprayed weedkiller along the fence on a windy day, and it had drifted over into her neighbor's vegetable beds. Within a week his lettuces were yellow and shriveled. The old man walked slowly along the rows, puzzled, lifting the leaves. He had no idea. Lale watched from her kitchen window with her arms wrapped around herself. He had been growing those vegetables since his wife died; it was the thing that got him out of bed. She knew she had to go over there and tell him, and her feet felt nailed to the floor.

When Teo was twelve he had trampled his grandmother's tulips during a game and told her a dog had done it. She had believed him. Now she was gone, and he was planting tulip bulbs in her old garden, kneeling in the damp soil, and the memory came back sharp and whole. Such a small lie, thirty years ago. Why did it press on him now, in his chest, making his hands clumsy with the bulbs. He thought of her face that day, trusting him completely, and he wanted, uselessly, to go back and tell her the truth.

Nell sat in the clinic waiting room with her son, who had a burn on his arm from the kettle. She had left it on the edge of the counter while she answered a message. Just for a moment. He was being brave now, swinging his legs, but he had screamed at the time, and that sound kept returning to her. Her chest felt tight and her hands would not stop moving in her lap. When the nurse asked what had happened, Nell told her plainly, every detail, and could hardly get the words out past the lump in her throat.

Rafa had told his friend the lump was probably nothing and to stop fussing, because he had not wanted to drive him to the doctor that week. Two months later they sat together in this clinic hearing that it had spread. His friend said it did not matter, it would have been the same. Rafa did not believe it. He kept going back to that evening, his own voice saying it was nothing. His hands were cold and clammy. He wanted to say something, and every sentence he started fell apart in his mouth before it reached the air.

A card arrived in the mail from Wren's old friend, asking gently about the book she had lent her two years ago. My father gave me that book before he died, it said. Wren found it at the bottom of a box, its pages rippled and stained where she had spilled coffee across them and meant to replace it and never had. Her stomach dropped and her cheeks burned. She sat on the floor with the book in one hand and the card in the other, turning the stained pages, thinking of her friend's father, and not knowing how she would ever face her.

A letter came from the bank saying Amir's elderly aunt was overdrawn. He knew why. Last year he had borrowed money from her account, promising to pay it back within the month, and then there had been the car, and the holiday, and he had let it slide. She had never mentioned it. He sat at the kitchen table with the letter and did the sums, and they made his mouth go dry. She had been going without heating to cover it. He put his head in his hands. He had to call her, and he had to pay it all back today.

Gus had forgotten to fill the rabbit's water bottle before a long weekend away. When he came home on Monday the rabbit was lying still in the corner of its hutch, breathing shallowly. The vet said it would probably recover. Gus sat by the hutch that night with his hand resting on the soft fur, feeling the tiny rapid heartbeat. His own heart was pounding. He had packed his bag so carefully, and forgotten the one thing that mattered. He kept picturing the rabbit nosing at the empty bottle, hour after hour, waiting for him to come home.

Noor had shouted at the dog for chewing a shoe, and he had crept under the table and stayed there all evening, trembling. It was an old shoe. She had had a bad day and he had been the nearest thing. Now it was late and he still would not come out, and she lay on the kitchen floor on her side, holding out her hand, speaking softly. Her chest ached. He was only a dog; he did not understand anything except that she had turned on him. When at last he crept forward and licked her fingers, her throat closed up.

Before Hana moved out of the shared flat, she had left without paying her last month of rent, telling herself her flatmate could afford it. Now, unpacking in her new place, she found the old key in her coat pocket. Her flatmate had sent one short message, which she had not answered. Hana sat on a box and read it again: I thought we were friends. Her face went hot and her stomach turned over. The money was sitting in her account. She opened her banking app, and her thumb hovered, and she thought of all the evenings they had cooked together.

When Zeb moved house he gave away his late brother's guitar to a stranger online, just to have one less thing to carry. Only afterwards did his niece ask where it was. She had been saving to buy it from him. Zeb stood among the half-unpacked boxes in the new flat while she waited for an answer, and felt his face go hot. He could still see the stranger walking off with it under his arm. He had not even asked her. He spent the evening searching the listings and writing to the buyer again and again, offering double.

Cycling home in the dark, Jun had clipped a boy on a scooter at the crossing, and the boy had fallen and scraped his knees. Jun had shouted that he should look where he was going and ridden off. Now he sat on the edge of his bed, still in his helmet, going over it. The boy's mother had called after him. He had been the one on the wrong side of the road. His heart was still racing and his face was hot. He took off the helmet and set it down, and thought about the boy's bleeding knees, and the way he had ridden off.

Quin had borrowed his friend's racing bicycle and left it unlocked outside the bakery for five minutes. It was gone when he came out. His friend had saved for a year to buy it. Quin walked the streets for an hour looking, then stood outside his friend's door with his hand raised to knock, unable to do it. His stomach churned. He kept going over it, the moment he had decided a lock was not worth the bother. When the door finally opened he could not meet his friend's eyes and stared at the doormat, his mouth dry.

At the market the stall holder had given Vera change for a fifty when she had paid with a twenty. She noticed on the bus home, counting coins. The woman at the stall was old and sold eggs from her own hens, and her money tin had looked nearly empty. Vera turned the extra notes over in her hands. She could keep them; no one would know. But her stomach felt sour, and she kept picturing the old woman counting up at the end of the day and coming up short. At the next stop she got off and waited for a bus back.

Femi had knocked over a crate of peaches at the market while arguing on his phone and walked away without a word, leaving the young seller to pick up the bruised fruit. Halfway down the street he looked back and saw her kneeling on the cobbles, sorting the damaged peaches from the good. His neck prickled with heat. Those were probably a day's profit. He stood still among the shoppers, his phone still in his hand, and felt the weight of it settle in his gut. Then he turned around and walked back toward her stall, reaching for his wallet.

It was raining, and Una was stuck indoors with the diary she had found in her daughter's room and read without asking. She had put it back exactly where it was. Now, at the window, she kept going over the private things she had seen, things she had no right to know. Her daughter would be home at five and would never find out. That made it no better. Una's chest felt tight and her hands would not keep still. She knew she would have to tell her what she had done, and she did not know how to begin.

On a wet Sunday Dara scrolled back through old messages and found the one from her friend three years ago, asking for help moving house after her husband left. Dara had not replied. She had meant to. Then her friend had moved away and they had lost touch. Rain drummed on the skylight. Dara read the message again, the little plea at the end, and felt heat rise up her neck. She pictured her friend alone carrying boxes down the stairs. Her thumb hovered over the keyboard for a long time. What could she possibly write, three years too late.

Ivo's friend came to visit and mentioned, lightly, that she had not been invited to his wedding. She laughed it off, but her eyes did not. Ivo had left her off the list to save money, and had told himself she would not mind. Now she was sitting in his kitchen, bringing a gift for the baby, and he could not stop thinking of the photos she must have seen. His ears went hot and his coffee tasted bitter. He tried to explain, and the words came out wrong, flimsy, and he could see she knew exactly what they were worth.

Before his friend arrived, Eli hid the expensive camera he had borrowed a year ago and broken, telling himself he would get it repaired first. His friend sat down on the sofa and asked, casually, whether he had finished with it yet; he needed it for his sister's wedding. Eli said it was at his parents' house. The lie came out smooth, and then sat in the room between them all afternoon. Eli's stomach was knotted. Every time his friend smiled at him, it tightened. After the visit he took the broken camera out of the cupboard and stared at it.

Sami had sold his old car to a young student without telling her the gearbox was failing. He had known; the mechanic had warned him. She had paid in cash, counting it out carefully from an envelope, clearly her savings. Now she had called: the car had broken down on the motorway, and she asked, bewildered, if he had any idea what could have happened. Sami said no. After he hung up he stood in the hallway with the phone in his hand and his heart pounding, knowing he would have to call her back and give her the money.

Driving his father's old car, Oren had reversed into the garden wall, and when his father asked about the dent he said a neighbor must have hit it. His father went next door to ask. Now Oren could hear them through the window, his father's puzzled voice, the neighbor's firm denial. His father came back in shaking his head and said he could not understand people anymore. Oren stood at the sink with his back to him. His face burned. He turned off the tap and made himself turn around to tell him.

Bea was forty minutes late picking up her son from school because she had stayed for a drink after work and lost track of time. When she arrived he was sitting alone on the steps with a teacher, his coat buttoned wrong, his eyes red. He did not say anything, just took her hand. On the drive home he fell asleep in the back seat. Bea kept glancing at him in the mirror, her grip tight on the wheel. He had been waiting all that time, watching every car. She would never let that happen again, she told herself, and could not stop seeing him on those steps.

Tavi had promised his daughter he would come to her school play, and then worked late. He arrived at the gate as the other parents were leaving, carrying programs and flowers. She came out in her costume, a paper star on her head, and looked past him for a moment before she saw him. She said it was fine. It was not fine. Walking home, she held his hand and told him every line she had said, and his chest ached with every word, because he should have been in that room, watching her say them.

On the beach Rhea had told her little brother she would watch his things while he swam, and then had wandered off to buy ice cream. When she came back his phone and wallet were gone. He stood dripping on the towel, staring at the empty spot, and did not shout at her, which was worse. Rhea felt her face go hot and her stomach drop. It had been the phone he saved for all summer. She kept going over it, the moment she had got up and walked away, and she emptied her own purse into his hands.

Years ago at the lake, Yara had dared her cousin to jump from the high rock, and he had broken his leg in two places. He had limped for a long time after. Now, visiting the lake again with her own children, she stood below that same rock, looking up at it. The water was flat and bright. Her cousin had never once mentioned it. Her chest tightened and she felt the old sick heaviness settle in her stomach. She had been the one who laughed and pushed. She called her children away from the rocks, sharply, and they looked at her, puzzled.
